Paper_name: Relevant for Us? We-Prioritization in Cognitive Processing
Summary: This study investigates whether humans prioritize processing information relevant to their own group ('We') over information relevant to an out-group ('They'), even without immediate collaborative goals. Three experiments used a shape-label matching task where participants were assigned to groups based on common preference or arbitrarily. Results showed a consistent processing benefit for we-related information (we-prioritization) regardless of group induction type. A final experiment found this prioritization did not extend to other individual members of a short-term transitory group. The findings suggest an intrinsic predisposition to prioritize group-relevant information, which may optimize collaborative processes.
Author: Merryn D. Constable, Fruzsina Elekes, Natalie Sebanz, Günther Knoblich
Journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
Conclusion: The study demonstrates a robust we-prioritization effect, where information associated with one's own group is processed faster and more accurately than information associated with an out-group, even in ad hoc, transitory groups without explicit collaborative goals. This effect is distinct from self-prioritization, as it did not extend to familiar others within the group, challenging the 'extended self' hypothesis. The results indicate a top-down cognitive mechanism that prioritizes group-beneficial information, potentially supporting the 'we-mode' and optimizing readiness for joint action.
